---
title: "How Much Evidence Is Enough? A Framework for Managing Data Reuse and Analytical Uncertainty in Repeated Data Analysis"
---
**Presenter:** Alyssa Columbus, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Johns Hopkins University

**Co-authors:** Brian Caffo (Johns Hopkins University), Martin Lindquist (Johns Hopkins University)

### Abstract {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Large-scale datasets are increasingly reused across many studies to test new hypotheses, revisit prior findings, or explore alternative analytic decisions. While reuse enables discovery and efficiency, each analysis involves a sequence of reasonable but non-equivalent choices, including model specification, covariate adjustment, preprocessing, and inclusion criteria. Across repeated uses, these choices accumulate and can produce substantial variability in results, increasing the likelihood of false positives, unstable estimates, and conclusions that depend on arbitrary decisions. Despite growing attention to reproducibility, no widely adopted framework exists for assessing how much reliable evidence a dataset can support under repeated reuse. In practice, datasets are often treated as effectively inexhaustible, even when successive analyses yield diminishing informational returns.

This work develops a principled framework for evaluating the evidential yield of a dataset under repeated and flexible analysis. Building on multiverse analysis, specification curve analysis, and the vibration of effects framework, we treat a dataset as generating evidence through analyses drawn from a space of reasonable analytic choices. We define this analysis space to capture variation in model form, covariate sets, transformations, and inclusion criteria, and assess stability by examining the distribution of results across it. We then introduce evidential yield, defined as the new information gained from additional analyses relative to prior ones, operationalized by tracking how the distribution of results evolves as analyses accumulate. When additional analyses no longer materially change this distribution, diminishing returns indicate the dataset has been extensively explored for the question at hand.

The framework incorporates structured replication strategies, including exploratory–confirmatory partitioning and cross-dataset comparisons, implemented as reproducible R workflows. Initial applications use specification curve and multiverse analyses, with ongoing simulation studies examining how evidential yield metrics respond to varying signal, noise, and model misspecification.
